questions.question:
Statement I : A charged body can attract an uncharged body.
Statement II : A charged body can induce charges of opposite signs on uncharged body.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, and Statement II is the correct explanation of the Statement I.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, but Statement II is not the correct explanation of the Statement I.
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct.
questions.explanation:
Generated by Allie

Problem Statement: The question asks us to evaluate two statements related to electrostatics: Statement I says a charged body can attract an uncharged body, and Statement II says a charged body can induce charges of opposite signs on an uncharged body. Then, it asks us to determine if both statements are true and if Statement II correctly explains Statement I.

Underlying Concept: The core concept involved is electrostatic induction (polarization). When a charged object is near a neutral (uncharged) body, it causes a redistribution of charges inside the neutral body, creating induced charges of opposite sign on the side closer to the charged body. This induction leads to an attractive force between them despite the neutral body having zero net charge.

Tips and Tricks: Remember that neutral objects can still experience forces due to induced charges caused by nearby charged objects. The attraction is due to induced polarization, not an overall change in net charge.

Common Mistakes: A common mistake is to assume an uncharged body cannot be attracted by a charged body because it has no net charge. Students might also confuse induction with actual transfer of charge.

Why Other Options Are Incorrect?: Options stating that Statement II is incorrect ignore the well-known principle of electrostatic induction. Similarly, claiming Statement I is false contradicts observed phenomena of attraction between charged and neutral bodies.
